title: Trump's Move to Import Cheap Beef Sparks Backlash From GOP Ranching States
excerpt: The president paused tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of ground beef imports to cut grocery prices, but Republican lawmakers and cattle ranchers say the plan undermines domestic producers.
body:
• Trump announced a 90-day tariff pause allowing 300,000 metric tons of foreign ground beef into the U.S. at a 25% discount
  • Republican senators from ranching states — including South Dakota, Montana, and Nebraska — publicly opposed the move
  • Beef prices are up 9.4% year-over-year, with the average price reaching $6.89 per pound
  • The National Cattlemen's Beef Association warned the plan would undermine efforts to rebuild the domestic herd

President Donald Trump's plan to lower grocery prices by opening the door to cheaper foreign beef imports has triggered an unusual revolt from within his own party, with Republican lawmakers from ranching states warning the move will devastate American cattle producers.

Trump announced Friday on Truth Social that the U.S. will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to enter the country tariff-free over the next 90 days. In exchange, foreign exporters agreed to sell their product at a 25% discount. The president is expected to sign an executive order within two weeks formalizing the arrangement.

Republicans Push Back

The reaction from GOP lawmakers was swift and uncharacteristically sharp.

https://x.com/RedWavePress/status/2090807728012673176

"This hurts! American cattle producers have been disadvantaged for far too long. What our market really needs is a stable, America-First national policy that promotes American beef rather than continuing to import foreign beef as a quick 'fix.'"

— Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D.

Sen. Deb Fischer of Nebraska said the country cannot lower grocery prices "at the expense of American producers." Sen. Tim Sheehy of Montana acknowledged Trump's "heart is in the right place" but said importing beef will "harm our ranching families who feed the nation."

In the House, Rep. Julie Fedorchak of North Dakota warned that lower grocery prices should not come "on the backs of North Dakota ranchers and producers," noting the timing is particularly harmful as many ranchers are bringing feeder cattle to market.

Rising Prices, Shrinking Herds

Beef and veal prices were up 9.4% in July compared to the previous year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The average price per pound reached $6.89, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Stubborn food inflation poses a major political challenge for Trump and congressional Republicans heading into November's midterm elections.

The domestic cattle herd has shrunk to multi-decade lows following years of drought, the spread of the parasitic New World screwworm near the Mexican border, and limits on cattle from Mexico. Imported beef has surged 122% over five years, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation.

The National Cattlemen's Beef Association criticized the plan directly. "Flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd," the group said.

A Balancing Act Before Midterms

Trump framed the move as a consumer-friendly measure. "This deal will reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again," he posted on Truth Social.

But agricultural economists say the approach carries contradictions. High cattle prices are what incentivize ranchers to expand their herds — a biological process that takes roughly two years. Flooding the market with imports could suppress those prices, discouraging the very herd rebuilding Trump says he wants.

The USDA estimates that four major companies buy about 85% of U.S. steers and heifers. Research suggests their market power, combined with limited processing capacity, may be driving down the prices ranchers receive even as consumers pay record prices at the grocery store.

Virginia Farm Bureau President Scott Sink urged the administration to reduce costs for fuel, feed, and equipment instead. "Rebuilding the U.S. cattle herd takes time — it cannot happen overnight," Sink said.

Rep. Kat Cammack of Florida backed Trump's goal but drew a line: "Short-term relief can't come at the expense of American ranchers, free markets and long-term solutions."

What's Next

Trump is expected to sign the executive order within two weeks. Meanwhile, several Republican senators are pushing for mandatory country-of-origin labeling on beef, which would let consumers distinguish domestic from imported products — a measure the industry has sought for years.
nri_angle: Rising grocery prices directly affect Indian-American households, and the broader debate over food costs and trade policy carries implications for how inflation shapes the midterm landscape.
